newsitem.title: UK: New Russia Eurobond opens door for small investors.
newsitem.headline: New Russia Eurobond opens door for small investors.

text.p: Russia on Monday set plans for its second-ever international bond in March, a mark-denominated issue which will give small investors their first chance to buy high-yielding Russian debt.

Russia's deputy finance minister Mikhail Kasyanov told Reuters in Moscow the government would launch a 1.0 billion mark Eurobond in early March as part of a $3.0 billion fundraising programme expected in 1997.
Russia tapped the international capital markets for the first time since its 1917 revolution last November with a $1.0 billion five-year bond, the largest debut bond ever seen.

The deal was heavily oversubscribed despite being priced to yield 3.45 percentage points above U.S. Treasury notes, below the market's expectations, and showed Russia there was heavy demand for its debt.

But whereas the first Eurobond was sold mainly to institutions such as pension funds and insurance companies, the new mark bond will give yield-hungry European retail investors a chance to buy Russian paper.
"If you have extensive marketing of the bond, like with Russia's dollar Eurobond, the mark deal will go very well," a syndicate manager at a European bank in Frankfurt said.
"Investors are really greedy for yield and also for the name. They are looking for new names in the Euromark sector."
Kasyanov said the mark bond would be mainly aimed at investors in Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Benelux.

Bankers said the issue could have a maturity of as much as seven years, two more than the five-year dollar bond sold in November and potentially reflecting increased confidence in Russia's status as a creditworthy borrower.
An official at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, which will underwrite the bond together with Credit Suisse First Boston, said the maturity would be five to seven years.

"The Russians will be interested in maturity extension," a banker involved in the dollar Eurobond said. "The mark sector, for high-yielding borrowers, has provided long maturities. For example, Argentina issued 30-year paper there last year."
Russian debt rallied on Monday on news of the Eurobond and on plans Russia would reschedule its London Club debt by the end of March or early April.
Continued uncertainty about the state of President Boris Yeltsin's health was not worrying the market.

The success of the Russian Eurobond sold in November far exceeded market expectations, which were initially for a bond of as little as around $300 million. The bond, which had been talked about for some two years, came to the market after extensive economic reforms in Russia began to kick in.
